421.title: Before I formed thee (Jeremiah 1)
421.hook: a young man says I am a child, and God says I knew thee before
421.howItsDone: Catholics hear Jeremiah's call at Mass, and the Catechism cites Jeremiah 1:5 in its teaching on the dignity of human life from conception.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the eved, the servant whose wounds heal others. Your line was by his bruises. A new week, and a new prophet.

He comes from a family of priests in Anathoth, in the land of Benjamin. The book dates him from the thirteenth year of King Josiah until Jerusalem is carried away captive. He's young; how young, nobody knows, since the text only lets him call himself a boy. And he's about to be handed a hard job: to tell his own people, year after year, that disaster is coming, to watch them ignore him, and then to watch it happen. His name is Jeremiah, Jeremias in the Douay-Rheims. And it begins with something about before he was born.
screen: `A PRIEST'S SON FROM ANATHOTH.` → `THE THIRTEENTH YEAR OF JOSIAH.` → `A HARD JOB.`

segments.voice: The word of the Lord comes to him, in the Douay-Rheims: "Before I formed thee in the bowels of thy mother, I knew thee: and before thou camest forth out of the womb, I sanctified thee, and made thee a prophet unto the nations." Notice the order. Known first. Then set apart. Then given a job. Before Jeremiah did anything, he was known. His answer is honest. In the Douay: "Ah, ah, ah, Lord God: behold, I cannot speak, for I am a child." Stammering. God doesn't argue about his age: say not, I am a child. You'll go where I send you. Be not afraid, for I am with thee. Then God touches his mouth, the way the coal touched Isaiah's lips: I have given my words in thy mouth. Then a strange little test. What do you see, Jeremiah? A branch of an almond tree. Good, God says, for I am watching over my word. In Hebrew it's a pun: almond is shaqed, watching is shoqed. Some readers explain the name: the almond wakes early in spring, the watchful tree. The Douay, following the Latin, simply calls it a rod watching. The Church has taken that first line further than Jeremiah's own story: the Catechism quotes it in teaching that human life is to be respected and protected from the moment of conception. For Jeremiah, the knowing came first, before all the hard years.

segments.voice: Set down, one at a time, the things you usually use to explain who you are: your job, your mistakes, your age, what people think of you. Underneath them all, Jeremiah heard something older. If you pray, rest in his line, before I formed thee, I knew thee; if you don't, simply let yourself be for a moment, without needing to earn it.

422.title: The potter (Jeremiah 18)
422.hook: a vessel spoiled in the potter's hand is made again
422.howItsDone: Catholics bring what has gone wrong in their lives to God in the sacrament of penance and in daily prayer, and Jeremiah's visit to the potter's house is among the readings at weekday Mass.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the shaqed, an almond branch, and a young man known before he was formed. Your line was known before the womb.

Anyone who has tried a pottery class knows the moment. The clay is spinning, it's rising, it actually looks like a bowl, and then one wobble and the whole wall folds over like a tired flower. The instructor doesn't hand you new clay. She says: squash it, wet it, center it again. Jeremiah watched that moment about twenty-six centuries ago. God sent him on an errand with no explanation: go down to the potter's house, and you'll hear my words there. So he stood in a workshop and watched a craftsman ruin a pot.
screen: `ONE WOBBLE, AND THE BOWL FOLDS.` → `GO DOWN TO THE POTTER'S HOUSE.` → `A PROPHET WATCHES A POT FAIL.`

segments.voice: The potter is at his wheel, and the vessel he's shaping goes wrong in his hands. He doesn't throw the clay out. He gathers it up and makes another vessel from the same lump, as it seemed good to him. Then the word comes, a question first: can't I do with you what this potter does? And in the Douay-Rheims: "Behold as clay is in the hand of the potter, so are you in my hand, O house of Israel." Two things are true at once in that workshop. The clay is soft, so it can go wrong. And because it's still soft, it can be made again. A word is hiding here from yesterday. The Hebrew for potter, yotser, means one who forms, from the same verb as before I formed thee. The God who formed Jeremiah in the womb is the potter still at the wheel. The message wasn't only comfort, though. The next verses warn a whole nation: if a people turns from its evil, God will relent; if it turns from good, the good is taken back. And in the next chapter Jeremiah buys a finished, fired jar and smashes it in front of the elders. A fired pot can't be reworked. Many Catholics think of this chapter when they bring what has gone wrong to God, in the sacrament of penance, in an evening examen, in a quiet church. The pot that slumped isn't the end of the clay.

segments.voice: Cup your hands in your lap as if you were holding a lump of wet clay, and let something that went wrong come to mind: a conversation that collapsed, a habit that slumped, a plan that folded on the wheel. Don't fix it; just hold it, and notice it's still soft. If you pray, hold your hands out and give it back to God as it is.
The potter. In Jeremiah, the craftsman who doesn't throw away spoiled clay but makes it into another vessel. Today's word.
Your line: made again. Same clay, another vessel, still soft. That's day four hundred twenty-two.

423.title: A new covenant (Jeremiah 31:31–34)
423.hook: a law written on hearts, not stone; the words echo at every Mass
423.howItsDone: At every Mass the priest speaks over the chalice of the blood of the new and eternal covenant, and Jeremiah 31:31–34 is read in the Church's lectionary, including in Lent.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the potter's house: a spoiled pot shaped again from the same clay. Your line was made again.

Jerusalem is surrounded. The Temple will burn. And in the middle of all that bad news, a prophet is told to write down a promise. It holds a phrase Catholics hear over the chalice at every Mass: the blood of the new and eternal covenant. New compared to what? That word didn't start at the Last Supper. It started with Jeremiah, in a city about to fall. Some scholars call these chapters the Book of Consolation.
screen: `A PROMISE IN A FALLING CITY.` → `THE BLOOD OF THE NEW COVENANT.` → `NEW COMPARED TO WHAT?`

segments.voice: In the Douay-Rheims: "Behold the days shall come, saith the Lord, and I will make a new covenant with the house of Israel, and with the house of Juda." Not like the old one, made when God took their fathers by the hand to lead them out of Egypt, the one they broke. That covenant was written on stone, two tablets carried down a mountain. This time the writing moves: "I will give my law in their bowels, and I will write it in their heart." Bowels sounds odd to us, but in older English it meant the innermost part of a person, the gut, where you feel things before you think them. The law won't be outside you, pressing in. It'll be inside you, pressing out. No one will need to teach his neighbor, saying know the Lord, because all of them will know me, from the least to the greatest, and I will forgive their sin and remember it no more. Centuries later, Luke tells us, Jesus took the cup at supper and said, in the Douay: "This is the chalice, the new testament in my blood." In the Bible, testament and covenant translate the same word: berit in Hebrew, diatheke in Greek, testamentum in Latin. That's where the name New Testament comes from. The Letter to the Hebrews quotes Jeremiah's whole passage. Catholics hear it fulfilled in Christ and renewed at every Mass. Jews read it as God's lasting promise to Israel and Judah, and the Catholic Church teaches that God's covenant with the Jewish people has never been revoked.

segments.voice: Put a hand on your chest if you like, and think of one thing you know is right without anyone telling you: telling a friend the truth, not mocking someone who's down, keeping a promise. Some readers hear Jeremiah's promise in that kind of writing. If you pray, thank God for what's written there, and ask for what's still blank.

424.title: New every morning (Lamentations 3:22–23)
424.hook: in the ruins, the mercies of the Lord are not consumed
424.howItsDone: Catholics have sung passages of Lamentations at Tenebrae during Holy Week, and some Catholics begin the day with a morning offering or Morning Prayer, thanking God before anything else.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a new covenant: the law moved from stone into the innermost part of a person. Your line was written on the heart.

Here's a strange fact about grief: someone once wrote it out in alphabetical order. The Book of Lamentations is five poems about Jerusalem after the Babylonians burned it. The walls are down, the Temple is ash, children beg for bread in the streets. And four of the five poems are acrostics: each verse, or each set of verses, starts with the next letter of the Hebrew alphabet, from aleph to tav. Maybe it was a way to hold sorrow that has no shape. And right in the middle of the middle poem, something turns.
screen: `GRIEF IN ALPHABETICAL ORDER.` → `A CITY IN ASHES.` → `IN THE MIDDLE, SOMETHING TURNS.`

segments.voice: Chapter three is the longest poem, sixty-six verses, three for each letter. A man says, in effect: I am the one who has seen affliction. He's been walled in, weighed down with chains, his prayers shut out, his teeth broken on gravel. His hope, he says, has perished. Then at verse twenty-one: this I call back to mind, and so I have hope. And then, in the Douay-Rheims: "The mercies of the Lord that we are not consumed: because his commiserations have not failed. They are new every morning, great is thy faithfulness." Commiserations is an old word for compassion. In Hebrew it's rachamim, which shares its root with the word for womb, and some readers hear a mother's love in it. Notice what the poet doesn't say. He doesn't say the city is fine. The ruins are still there when he looks up. He says the mercies are not used up. Like manna in the desert, they don't keep overnight; they come new each morning, enough for the day. Tradition gives the book to Jeremiah, though the poems name no author. In the older Holy Week services called Tenebrae, Catholics sang Lamentations in the dark, candles going out one by one. Jews read it on Tisha B'Av, the day of mourning for the Temple. Both keep this book for the worst days, because it doesn't pretend. It just finds, in the middle of the alphabet, one thing that hasn't run out.
screen: `I AM THE ONE WHO HAS SEEN AFFLICTION.` · `THIS I CALL TO MIND.` · `RACHAMIM: A MOTHER'S COMPASSION.` · `THE RUINS ARE STILL THERE.` · then, large: `THEY ARE NEW EVERY MORNING.`

segments.voice: Look back over the last day for one mercy that came anyway, in the middle of everything else: a text from someone, hot water, a person who was kind on a bad day. Hold it for a moment, and let tomorrow's first words, before the phone, be thank you for one thing. If you pray, it can be to God, with this line from Lamentations.
rachamim. Hebrew for compassion, kin to the word for womb: the Lord's mercies that aren't used up, but come fresh each morning. Today's word.

425.title: The dry bones (Ezekiel 37)
425.hook: a valley of bones rattles, joins, and breathes
425.howItsDone: The Catholic Church reads Ezekiel's vision of the dry bones at the Vigil of Pentecost and on a Sunday in Lent, hearing in it the promise of resurrection and the gift of the Holy Spirit.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a poem from the ashes of Jerusalem, and rachamim: his mercies are new every morning. Your line was his mercies are new.

Ezekiel was a priest, carried off to Babylon with King Joachin, years before the city fell. He lived among the exiles by a river called the Chobar, a long way from home. That's where his visions came, and they were strange. Wheels full of eyes. A scroll he was told to eat. And this one. The hand of the Lord sets him down in the middle of a valley full of bones. Very many, the text says. And very dry.
screen: `A PRIEST IN EXILE.` → `SET DOWN IN A VALLEY.` → `VERY MANY, AND VERY DRY.`

segments.voice: God walks him round about them, so he sees how many there are. Then a question, in the Douay-Rheims: "Son of man, dost thou think these bones shall live?" It's a real question, and Ezekiel hands it back: "O Lord God, thou knowest." So God tells him to preach to the bones: ye dry bones, hear the word of the Lord. As he speaks there's a rattling, and the bones come together, bone to its bone. Sinews come, then flesh, then skin. And they lie there. Bodies, but no breath. So God tells him to prophesy a second time, to the breath: come from the four winds, and blow upon these slain, that they may live. Breath comes into them, and they stand up on their feet, an exceeding great army. The chapter turns on one Hebrew word, ruach. It means breath, and wind, and spirit. Ezekiel uses it all three ways here, sometimes in one sentence, and English has to pick one each time. Then God explains: these bones are the whole house of Israel, the exiles saying our bones are dried up, our hope is lost. The vision promises that a people who thought they were finished would live and go home. Christians also hear in it the resurrection of the dead and the gift of the Spirit; the Church reads it at the Vigil of Pentecost and in Lent. Either way, the bones don't argue their way back to life. They're spoken to, and then breathed into.

segments.voice: Let one dried-out thing come to mind: a friendship gone quiet, a hope you stopped mentioning, a part of your faith that hasn't moved in a long time. Don't try to make it live; just ask over it, can this live?, and give Ezekiel's answer, thou knowest, as you breathe. If you pray, pray over it as it is.

426.title: I will allure her (Hosea 2)
426.hook: God as a hurt husband who leads his people into the wilderness to speak to her heart
426.howItsDone: Catholics hear Hosea's promise to speak to the heart in the Mass readings, and Catholic retreats sometimes take it up, describing days of silence as being led into the wilderness to listen.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Ezekiel's valley: bone to its bone, then ruach, breath, from the four winds. Your line was can these bones live.

Hosea's message came to him as a marriage. The book dates him by the kings he lived under, among them Jeroboam of Israel, and it opens with God telling him to marry a woman who would be unfaithful to him. Her name was Gomer. They had three children, and each got a name that was a sermon. A son called Jezrahel, after a valley of bloodshed. A daughter called Without mercy. A son called Not my people. Every time he called them in for dinner, he said a prophecy out loud.
screen: `A PROPHET HANDED A MARRIAGE.` → `GOMER, AND THREE NAMES.` → `WITHOUT MERCY. NOT MY PEOPLE.`

segments.voice: Chapter two sounds like a divorce court. The husband is God, the wife is the people, and the charge is that she ran after other lovers, the Baals, the local gods, and gave them the credit for her grain and wine and oil. The anger is real, and it goes on for verses. Then: therefore. And in the Douay-Rheims: "Therefore, behold I will allure her, and will lead her into the wilderness: and I will speak to her heart." Not punish her. Allure her. Win her back. The wilderness isn't exile; it's where the love story began, when God led the people out of Egypt and they were young. Speak to her heart is a Hebrew phrase for speaking tenderly, the way you talk to someone you've hurt, or who has hurt you. Joseph speaks to his brothers' hearts when he forgives them in Genesis; Isaiah is told to speak to the heart of Jerusalem. By the end of the chapter, God promises: I will espouse thee to me for ever, in justice and mercy and faithfulness. The children's names are reversed. Without mercy will be shown mercy. Not my people will hear: thou art my people. Some Catholic writers have read Hosea alongside the Song of Songs, as God's love for his people and for each soul. Some readers today find the picture hard, the wife cast as the one at fault and the anger so fierce, and they wrestle with that honestly. Either way, the turn is in the text: after all of it, therefore, tenderness.
screen: `A CHARGE LIKE A DIVORCE COURT.` · `THEREFORE: I WILL ALLURE HER.` · `SPEAK TO HER HEART: SPEAK TENDERLY.` · `NOT MY PEOPLE BECOMES MY PEOPLE.` · then, large: `I WILL SPEAK TO HER HEART.`

segments.voice: Think of the last time you got something wrong, and the voice that started up afterward: a judge, a sigh, a list. Now picture the voice Hosea describes, the one that says therefore and turns gentle, leading you somewhere quiet. If you pray, let God speak to your heart; if you don't, speak to yourself the way you'd speak to a friend.
Gomer. Hosea's unfaithful wife, whose story became God's promise to lead his people into the wilderness and win them back with tenderness. Today's word.
Your line: speak to her heart. Not my people becomes my people. That's four hundred twenty-six.

427.title: Justice like a torrent (Amos 5:21–24)
427.hook: God doesn't want songs without justice for the poor
427.howItsDone: Catholic parishes join worship with works of justice and mercy, and Catholic social teaching, drawing on prophets like Amos, speaks of a preferential option for the poor.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Hosea and Gomer: after all the anger, therefore, tenderness. Your line was speak to her heart. Today the week ends.

In August 1963, on the steps of the Lincoln Memorial, Martin Luther King Jr. reached for the words of a shepherd from the eighth century before Christ. His name was Amos. He said himself he wasn't a prophet or a prophet's son; he was a herdsman who tended fig trees, from a small town called Tekoa in the south. God sent him north, to Bethel, the royal shrine of the kingdom of Israel, in a time of money and peace. The festivals were full, the music magnificent. And Amos stood up in the middle of it with a message nobody wanted.
screen: `1963, THE LINCOLN MEMORIAL.` → `A HERDSMAN FROM TEKOA.` → `FULL FESTIVALS AT BETHEL.`

segments.voice: Amos speaks in God's voice, and it's blunt. I hate your feast days. I won't accept your offerings. Take away the noise of your songs; I won't listen to the music of your harps. But read the chapters around it. Amos has just described people who sell the poor for a pair of shoes, who trample the heads of the needy into the dust, who take bribes at the town gate where justice was meant to be done. The problem isn't singing. It's singing at the festival and cheating at the market the next morning. Then the line King quoted, in the Douay-Rheims: "judgment shall be revealed as water, and justice as a mighty torrent." The Hebrew picture is exact. Most streams in that land are wadis, dry gullies that roar after a storm and are empty by summer. Amos asks for a nachal eitan, a stream that never fails. Not justice that flares up when a cause trends and is gone in a month. Justice that runs all year. Catholic social teaching speaks of a preferential option for the poor, and this is one of its roots. Look back at the week: a boy known before he was formed, a potter remaking clay, a covenant written on the heart, mercies new every morning, bones that breathe, a husband who speaks tenderly, and a stream that doesn't dry up. Seven pictures of a God who keeps coming back, and wants his people to keep coming back to the poor.
screen: `TAKE AWAY THE NOISE OF YOUR SONGS.` · `THE POOR SOLD FOR A PAIR OF SHOES.` · `NOT A WADI: A STREAM THAT NEVER FAILS.` · `A WEEK OF PROPHETS, LOOKED BACK ON.` · then, large: `JUSTICE AS A MIGHTY TORRENT.`

segments.voice: Let a prayer, hymn or song you love play in your head for a moment. Then think of one person near you who is treated unfairly, or poor and overlooked, and of one concrete thing, a fair word, a shared meal, a bill paid on time, that would let a little justice flow their way. If you pray, offer the song and the person together.
nachal eitan. Hebrew for an ever-flowing stream: Amos's demand that justice for the poor run like that, never drying up. Today's word.
Your line: justice that runs all year. A stream, not a wadi. Day four hundred twenty-seven, and the week, done.
